hypothesis: An adversary who compromised Windows hosts in this network stole credentials from them (MITRE ATT&CK tactic: Credential Access).

assessments.reason: Rar.exe from Temp by pbeesly's PowerShell created password-protected working.zip archives.
Wiped Rar.exe and staged working.zip on nashua.
Lateral movement to NASHUA with plaintext credentials.
Anti-forensic deletion of dropped .scr, Draft.Zip and SysinternalsSuite.zip on scranton.
Defender service; LSASS handle is normal scanning.
Screensaver-named payload launched by explorer.exe that wrote monkey.png used by the IEX stego loader.
Compiled in-memory payload DLLs qkbkqqbs.dll and 0piklvia.dll from PowerShell.
Started via -verb runas as elevation proxy before registry Invoke-Expression loader.
Three cmd.exe-launched sdclt runs just before the csc.exe payload compile; known UAC-bypass proxy.

frame.restated: An adversary with existing access to Windows hosts on this network harvested credentials from those hosts.
frame.what_would_confirm: LSASS memory access or dumping (e.g., procdump, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, Mimikatz), SAM/SECURITY hive or NTDS.dit extraction, credential-store or DPAPI access, Kerberoasting/AS-REP roasting, or suspicious access to lsass.exe by non-standard processes.
frame.what_would_refute: No evidence of credential-dumping tooling, LSASS access, registry hive or NTDS.dit extraction, or anomalous authentication material access on any compromised host.

verdict.rule: Confirmed if >=1 in-scope incident of verified malicious findings (confidence >= medium); Inconclusive if only suspicious incidents or coverage gaps; Refuted if full coverage and no malicious/suspicious finding

T1003.name: OS Credential Dumping
T1003.reason: Sysinternals credential tooling staged and used.

T1003.001.name: LSASS Memory
T1003.001.reason: Extra LSASS read by pbeesly's powershell.exe.

T1003.002.name: Security Account Manager
T1003.002.reason: Only SAM\SAM write is lsass.exe updating HKLM\SAM\SAM\Domains\Account\F; no reg save/esentutl/hive copies, no SAM/SECURITY object access.

T1003.003.name: NTDS
T1003.003.reason: No ntdsutil/vssadmin/diskshadow process, no ntds/.dit file creation, no NTDS object access, no SMB file names.

T1003.004.name: LSA Secrets
T1003.004.reason: No lsadump/secrets/reg save command lines or script blocks, no SECURITY\Policy\Secrets object access; samlib.dll loads are Microsoft-signed system DLLs.

T1003.005.name: Cached Domain Credentials
T1003.005.reason: No 4663 access on Cache/SECURITY objects and no cachedump/mscash references in any channel.

T1003.006.name: DCSync
T1003.006.reason: Zeek drsuapi traffic is only DRSBind/DRSCrackNames/DRSUnbind from 10.0.1.4 and 10.0.1.6 to 10.0.0.4; no DRSGetNCChanges and no dcsync/lsadump tooling in Windows logs.

T1040.name: Network Sniffing
T1040.reason: The only packet-capture activity is the Azure Network Watcher agent (NetworkWatcherAgent.exe -> netsh.exe trace start capture=yes, SYSTEM on scranton.dmevals.local, stopped 7s later). No pktmon/windump/tcpdump, no pcap/npcap/winpcap service installs, no PowerShell capture commands, and no ftp/telnet cleartext credential traffic in the zeek window. The genuine attacker tooling found (PsExec-launched C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe beaconing to 192.168.0.4:8443 and a steganographic PowerShell loader) is C2/execution, not network sniffing.

T1056.name: Input Capture
T1056.reason: Input capture tooling (screen capture) and full-access lsass handle with an unbacked remote thread were executed by PowerShell on scranton.dmevals.local in the same session as exfiltration scripts.

T1056.002.name: GUI Input Capture
T1056.002.reason: Screen capture job ran on scranton.

T1056.003.name: Web Portal Capture
T1056.003.reason: Zero hits for IIS/wwwroot/inetpub command lines, file access, PowerShell WebAdministration scripts or login/logon/signin HTTP URLs.

T1056.004.name: Credential API Hooking
T1056.004.reason: Anchored LSASS handle/remote thread; no new instances.

T1110.name: Brute Force
T1110.reason: Zero 4625 failed logons in windows.security; the only credential-validation event is a single successful 4776 (Status 0x0) for pbeesly on newyork. No repeated authentication attempts.

T1110.001.name: Password Guessing
T1110.001.reason: No failed-logon sequences and no password-guessing code; the matching 4104 blocks are certificate export, 7-Zip exfiltration and benign helper/help text.

T1110.002.name: Password Cracking
T1110.002.reason: On scranton.dmevals.local, hidden-window encoded PowerShell (PID 2976, user pbeesly) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF at 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z — full-access credential dumping for offline cracking; same session exported certificates and staged a 7z archive.

T1110.003.name: Password Spraying
T1110.003.reason: All 4648 explicit-credential logons use the single account pbeesly (plus machine/service accounts from winlogon/wininit/taskhostw); no one-password-many-accounts pattern.

T1110.004.name: Credential Stuffing
T1110.004.reason: No failed authentications and no credential-list iteration in script blocks; stuffing would require repeated 4625/4771 which are absent.

T1111.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
T1111.reason: No MFA/smart-card interception evidence: zero smart-card registry modifications (C130), no smart-card or MFA provider events in windows.other (only a routine 'Credential Guard configuration: 0x0, 0' message), and no PowerShell script blocks referencing SmartCard/MFA. The credential-access activity that is present on scranton (Get-PrivateKeys certificate .pfx export at 03:04:56 and PowerShell->lsass.exe access with 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff at 03:05:16) is credential/certificate theft, not MFA interception; 4648 events are pbeesly PSEXESVC logons to NASHUA and machine-account logons during a scranton reboot.

T1187.name: Forced Authentication
T1187.reason: Zeek shows 10.0.1.4 failing SMB to 192.168.0.4 on 445/139 (all REJ) and then falling back to HTTP port 80 using DavClnt and Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362, with repeated 401 challenges followed by 207/201/200/204 responses on PROPFIND/PUT/LOCK/PROPPATCH/UNLOCK against /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z — the signature of a host being coerced into NTLM authentication to an attacker WebDAV server. Windows-side SMB traffic in the other window is benign SYSTEM traffic to internal DC 10.0.0.4.

T1212.name: Exploitation for Credential Access
T1212.reason: On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) in the pbeesly intrusion chain opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff then 0x1fffff and winlogon.exe/LogonUI.exe/dwm.exe with 0x1fffff at 03:05:16, with an UNKNOWN call-trace module — full-access credential theft from LSASS and logon session memory, followed by wsmprovhost.exe on nashua opening lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff at 03:09:29 after pbeesly's Kerberos logon. Background svchost/Azure-agent LSASS handles (0x1000/0x1400) and OS-internal accesses are benign.

T1539.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
T1539.reason: No access to browser cookie/credential stores: zero Sysmon 10 process-access events targeting chrome/firefox/msedge/iexplore/brave/opera, zero Security 4663 object accesses on cookies/login data/user data/mozilla paths, and the only cookie-named file creation is an OS package INetCookies path written by svchost.exe. The 4688 hits are SearchProtocolHost.exe (Windows Search user-agent string) and the 4104 Invoke-Exfil script only archives the user's Downloads folder to a WebDAV share, never browser profile data.

T1552.name: Unsecured Credentials
T1552.reason: Plaintext credentials in scripts and files.

T1552.001.name: Credentials In Files
T1552.001.reason: passwordsDB file and plaintext credentials in tooling.

T1552.003.name: Shell History
T1552.003.reason: All four ConsoleHost_history/PSReadLine checks returned zero hits.

T1552.006.name: Group Policy Preferences
T1552.006.reason: All five Groups.xml/cpassword/SYSVOL checks returned zero hits; only routine svchost gpt.ini policy refresh seen.

T1555.name: Credentials from Password Stores
T1555.reason: Vault file touched only by lsass.exe.

T1555.003.name: Credentials from Web Browsers
T1555.003.reason: Cert private keys exported to .pfx on scranton.

T1555.004.name: Windows Credential Manager
T1555.004.reason: No cmdkey/vault/credman/DPAPI activity; SAM and lsass handle requests came from lsass.exe itself during normal service start, and the only Credential string was a Credential Guard status message.

T1555.005.name: Password Managers
T1555.005.reason: No KeePass/1Password/Bitwarden process, .kdbx file, memory access or script reference anywhere in the datasets.

T1556.name: Modify Authentication Process
T1556.reason: LSASS access hits are benign system/AV/telemetry readers (0x1000/0x1400) plus lsass start-up handles; the only full-access readers are the actor's PowerShell/WinRM credential dumping. No authentication-process modification.

T1556.001.name: Domain Controller Authentication
T1556.001.reason: No skeleton-key style patching on DCs; 4624/4648 logons show only machine accounts and pbeesly via PSEXESVC. High-privilege lsass handles came from PowerShell (scranton) and wsmprovhost (nashua) credential theft.

T1556.002.name: Password Filter DLL
T1556.002.reason: No password-filter DLL dropped or registered; only Sysinternals accesschk.exe writing passwordsDB. No 4657 Notification Packages/Lsa changes, no filter DLL loaded into lsass.

T1556.005.name: Reversible Encryption
T1556.005.reason: All reversible-encryption checks (Set-ADUser, Set-ADAccountControl, dsmod, 4739, 'Reversible' strings) returned zero hits.

T1556.006.name: Multi-Factor Authentication
T1556.006.reason: No 4739 policy-change events, no Set-ADAuthenticationPolicy command lines, no 5136/4662 directory changes.

T1556.007.name: Hybrid Identity
T1556.007.reason: No AzureAD/Connect-MsolService script blocks and no directory-service change events; Azure binaries seen are standard antimalware/telemetry agents.

T1556.008.name: Network Provider DLL
T1556.008.reason: No registry writes to any NetworkProvider key and no related DLL registration or service install.

T1557.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
T1557.reason: Zeek conn log shows non-vendor MAC 12:34:56:78:9a:bc answering for four distinct IPs (10.0.0.4, 10.0.1.6, 192.168.0.4, 192.168.0.5) while genuine hosts use 00:0d:3a:* MACs - an on-path device intercepting SMB/gssapi/kerberos traffic.

T1557.001.name: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
T1557.001.reason: NBT-NS/LLMNR queries for SCRANTON/NASHUA from 10.0.1.4 and 10.0.1.6 with no legitimate responder, and SMB auth sessions to 10.0.0.4/10.0.1.6 answered by the rogue MAC; relay inferred, no responder tooling or DNSClient tampering directly logged.

T1557.002.name: ARP Cache Poisoning
T1557.002.reason: Single MAC 12:34:56:78:9a:bc bound to four different IPs in the zeek capture is the signature of ARP cache poisoning; the poisoning host itself is not among the monitored Windows hosts.

T1557.003.name: DHCP Spoofing
T1557.003.reason: No DHCP server/client events (1341/1342/1020/1063), no UDP 67/68 traffic in zeek, no DHCP PowerShell cmdlets; the only ipconfig/netsh/arp executions are Azure guest-agent and Network Watcher telemetry on scranton.

T1558.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
T1558.reason: Host scranton.dmevals.local is clearly compromised (malicious .scr -> cmd -> PowerShell steganographic IEX loader -> csc.exe compile -> sdelete64 anti-forensics) and PowerShell opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff access at 03:05:16Z, a credential-dumping precursor. However no Kerberos ticket theft/forgery artifacts (RC4 tickets, forged TGTs, ticket files) were observed, so the ticket-specific step is unproven.

T1558.001.name: Golden Ticket
T1558.001.reason: All 4768/4769 events are AES256 (0x12) with pre-auth and Status 0x0; krbtgt tickets requested are normal renewals. No forged-TGT authentication, RC4 downgrade, or Kerberos error events beyond normal KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED.

T1558.002.name: Silver Ticket
T1558.002.reason: TGS requests target only machine accounts (NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, SCRANTON$, WEC$) and krbtgt, all AES256 with success; no RC4 downgrade or anomalous service-ticket use.

T1558.003.name: Kerberoasting
T1558.003.reason: No RC4 (0x17) TGS requests, no bulk/distinct SPN enumeration, and no Kerberoast tooling in PowerShell script blocks or process command lines.

T1558.004.name: AS-REP Roasting
T1558.004.reason: All 14 event 4768 TGT requests show PreAuthType 2 (pre-auth enabled); Zeek shows normal KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED then AES256 success. No AS-REP roasting tooling observed.

T1606.name: Forge Web Credentials
T1606.reason: No forged web credential artifacts were found. The credential-access activity present (LSASS access with 0x1F3FFF/0x1FFFFF by PowerShell on scranton and wsmprovhost on nashua, Credential Manager 5379 enumeration by pbeesly, PsExec with cleartext password to NASHUA) is credential theft/lateral movement, not web credential forging.

T1606.001.name: Web Cookies
T1606.001.reason: Only legitimate WebDAV client cookie handling (rundll32 davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie to 192.168.0.4/webdav) and a system INetCookies file creation; no browser cookie store access or cookie forgery, and the PowerShell cookie search returned zero hits.

T1606.002.name: SAML Tokens
T1606.002.reason: 4624 authentication packages are only Kerberos, Negotiate and NTLM; no SAML/ADFS token issuance or use appears in windows.security, and the only token-named objects are WindowsLive Credential Manager entries read via 5379.

T1621.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
T1621.reason: The 62 HTTP events (31 x 401) are a single Windows WebDAV-MiniRedir session from 10.0.1.4 to 192.168.0.4 where each 401 is followed by a successful authenticated retry and a final PUT 201 of /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z. No MFA/identity-provider endpoints appear in DNS (only internal AD and Microsoft/Windows Update names) or TLS (all server_name 192.168.0.4), there are zero 4625 failed logons, and no PowerShell script block references MFA/2FA/Authenticator (the only 'azure' matches are the benign xActiveDirectory DSC module manifest). No MFA request generation observed.

findings.title: Credential-access tooling staged on scranton by pbeesly (Sysinternals suite, accesschk, sdelete) alongside LSASS access
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local the account pbeesly ran a hands-on-keyboard intrusion between 02:56 and 03:07 UTC: SysinternalsSuite.zip was expanded and moved to C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite, accesschk.exe was executed, Invoke-Discovery, Invoke-Persistence (steps 1 and 2) and Get-PrivateKeys were invoked, screenshots and clipboard were captured, and sdelete64.exe was used to wipe C:\programdata\victim\???cod.3aka3.scr, $env:APPDATA\Draft.Zip and the SysinternalsSuite.zip. The same session produced the full-access LSASS handle requests at 03:05:16. The 4673 events show the malicious C:\ProgramData\victim\...scr and PowerShell using SeProfileSingleProcessPrivilege/SeTcbPrivilege. This is attacker credential-access activity, not normal system behaviour.

findings.title: Credential-access tooling staged on scranton
findings.summary: SysinternalsSuite staged and used (accesschk, sdelete64, PsExec64) by pbeesly's PowerShell.

findings.title: PowerShell.exe on scranton opened lsass.exe with full-access masks (0x1F3FFF / 0x1FFFFF) under user pbeesly
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 at 03:05:16 UTC, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) on scranton.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe (PID 736) twice within 31 ms with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF — PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS-style rights used for LSASS memory dumping, not the benign 0x1000/0x1400 query rights that dominate the 326 lsass access events. The security log independently records the same handle requests (4656, AccessMask 0x1fffff and 0x1f3fff, SubjectUserName pbeesly) plus a 4663 read (AccessMask 0x10) on \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe. This occurred in the middle of a hands-on-keyboard intrusion by pbeesly on scranton: SysinternalsSuite was unzipped and moved to C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite, accesschk.exe was run, Invoke-Discovery / Invoke-Persistence / Get-PrivateKeys were executed, and sdelete64 was used to wipe files. No .dmp file was written to disk in the window, so the dump may have been held in memory or the write was not captured.

findings.title: Invoke-ScreenCapture PowerShell function repeatedly captured the desktop on scranton.dmevals.local
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell script block b91c2ae7-3a03-49df-8d2a-4c42fc79df56 (EventID 4104, user pbeesly, path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\psversion.ps1, 2020-05-02T03:05:53Z) defines function Invoke-ScreenCapture, which starts a background job looping forever, uses System.Windows.Forms/System.Drawing CopyFromScreen to grab the full virtual screen and saves each capture as a random-named .bmp in $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads every 300 seconds. A second script block (0365cb7f-22ef-47e4-ad96-230ddc962939, 03:05:59Z) contains the same System.Windows.Forms/System.Drawing screen-capture body. This is GUI input/screen capture of the user's desktop, collected into the same Downloads folder that the Invoke-Exfil function later archives and uploads to \\192.168.0.4\webdav. No fake credential prompt was observed: the only credential/consent command-line hits were three legitimate consent.exe process creations.

findings.title: Invoke-ScreenCapture job on scranton
findings.summary: Screenshot job started at 03:05:53Z and removed at 03:07:54Z by pbeesly's PowerShell.

findings.title: PowerShell opened a full-access handle to lsass.exe and created a remote thread in it on scranton.dmevals.local
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 at 03:05:16.623Z on scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, process GUID {47ab858c-e1e4-5eac-b803-000000000400}) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and a CallTrace ending in UNKNOWN(000001996D252982) — i.e. code not backed by a known module. In the same second a second handle with GrantedAccess 0x1fffff was taken, and Sysmon EventID 8 recorded a CreateRemoteThread from that same PowerShell PID into lsass.exe (NewThreadId 912, StartAddress 0x00000117610E0000, StartModule '-', StartFunction '-'). Full-access process handles plus an unbacked remote thread in lsass is the classic credential-API-hooking / in-memory credential theft pattern. This PowerShell activity sits in the same session as the attacker tooling on the host: user pbeesly's script blocks in C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\psversion.ps1 include Invoke-ScreenCapture (03:05:53) and Invoke-Exfil, which compresses the Downloads folder with password 'lolol' and copies it to \\192.168.0.4\webdav using hardcoded credentials (03:08:02). By contrast, the other lsass handles in the dataset are benign: svchost.exe via lsm.dll (0x101001), wininit/csrss (0x1fffff, basesrv/CSRSRV), WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe and AntimalwareConfig.exe via CorperfmonExt.dll (0x1400), and a csrss.exe CreateRemoteThread into lsass whose StartFunction is CtrlRoutine in KERNELBASE.dll (console control, benign).

findings.title: LSASS handle and remote thread on scranton
findings.summary: Anchored LSASS handle/remote-thread activity; no new instances beyond the anchor.

findings.title: Credential dumping on scranton: hidden-window PowerShell stager opened lsass with full access (0x1FFFFF)
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, PID 2976 was created at 2020-05-02T02:58:44Z as powershell.exe running with -noni -noexit -ep bypass -window hidden and an encoded command that decodes a System.Drawing bitmap from C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png and IEXes the extracted bytes (steganographic loader), under user pbeesly. At 2020-05-02T03:05:16.623Z and 03:05:16.654Z that same process (SourceProcessId 2976, SourceImage C:\windows\system32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\PowerShell.exe) opened a handle to C:\windows\system32\lsass.exe (TargetProcessId 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and then 0x1FFFFF — full-access PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS, the access pattern used to read lsass memory and extract credentials/hashes for offline cracking. This is the only PowerShell-to-lsass access in the dataset with such access rights; the other 322 lsass accesses are svchost.exe/Azure telemetry agents with 0x1000/0x1400. In the same session pbeesly also ran Get-PrivateKeys (exporting all LocalMachine certificates to .pfx with password 'saribas') and Invoke-Exfil (7-Zip of the Downloads folder to %APPDATA%\OfficeSupplies.7z), and made repeated 4648 explicit-credential logons to nashua.dmevals.local via C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe. The 4656 handle requests on SAM/SECURITY/ntds.dit objects were all issued by lsass.exe itself (10 events), i.e. normal, and the 3 file-creation hits for *SECURITY* were only Prefetch files for SecurityHealthHost/Service/Systray — no hive or ntds.dit copy was observed.

findings.title: WebDAV forced authentication from 10.0.1.4 to 192.168.0.4 after SMB fallback (DavClnt / Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir)
findings.summary: In the Zeek window (2020-04-30 00:32:14–00:35:25Z), host 10.0.1.4 attempted SMB to 192.168.0.4 on TCP 445 and 139 ten times, all rejected (conn_state REJ, 0 bytes). It then immediately switched to HTTP on port 80 to the same host, where the client identified itself as 'DavClnt' (OPTIONS /, 403) and then 'Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362' for 61 requests. The WebDAV session shows the classic forced-authentication handshake: repeated PROPFIND to /webdav and /webdav/ answered with 401 challenges followed by 207 Multi-Status, then PROPFIND/PUT/LOCK/PROPPATCH/UNLOCK against a lure file '/webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z' (PUT 201/204, LOCK 200, PROPPATCH 207, UNLOCK 204). The 401-then-success pattern on each method is the server soliciting NTLM credentials from the Windows WebClient service, i.e. the victim host being coerced into authenticating to an attacker-controlled WebDAV server. All 62 HTTP requests in the dataset went to 192.168.0.4 and 61 of 62 used the WebDAV MiniRedir user agent, so this is not normal browsing traffic. The Windows-side SMB connections in the 2020-05-02 window are unrelated: all 66 Sysmon event.code 3 records on 445/139 come from process.executable 'System' (SYSTEM) to internal hosts 10.0.0.4 and a link-local IPv6 address, consistent with normal domain controller traffic. No .scf/.url/.library-ms lure files were created; the only .lnk creations were Explorer writing Recent shortcuts for pbeesly and a powershell.exe-created hostui.lnk in the StartUp folder on scranton.dmevals.local, which is persistence rather than forced authentication.

findings.title: PowerShell on SCRANTON opened LSASS and winlogon with full-access masks (0x1FFFFF/0x1F3FFF) during a pbeesly intrusion chain
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local the user pbeesly ran a hands-on-keyboard PowerShell intrusion: a malicious screen-saver C:\ProgramData\victim\cod.3aka3.scr launched from explorer.exe spawned cmd.exe/powershell.exe, followed by Invoke-Discovery, Invoke-Persistence, Invoke-ScreenCapture, Invoke-Exfil (7-Zip archive with password 'lolol'), sdelete64.exe wiping artifacts, and Invoke-SeaDukeStage -ComputerName NASHUA. At 2020-05-02T03:05:16 PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and then 0x1fffff, and in the same second opened winlogon.exe, LogonUI.exe, dwm.exe and multiple svchost.exe with 0x1fffff — a full-access credential-theft pattern (LSASS + interactive logon session memory) with an UNKNOWN call-trace module, not a signed security product. This is the credential-access step of the intrusion, immediately preceding lateral movement to NASHUA (wsmprovhost.exe on nashua opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff at 03:09:29 after pbeesly's Kerberos logon and SeDebugPrivilege 4672 events).

findings.summary: accesschk.exe created passwordsDB on scranton and scripts embed saribas, Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by and MyCozyPassw0rd!.

findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly, a hidden PowerShell (PID 2976, launched by control.exe /name Microsoft.BackupAndRestoreCenter at 02:58:44) decoded a steganographic payload from C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png and IEX'd it; the same session later opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (03:05:16) and ran Invoke-Exfil (script block b2b03a9c, 03:08:02) which 7-Zips the Downloads folder with password 'lolol' and copies it to \\192.168.0.4\webdav using hardcoded credentials. findings.summary: Across the windows.security window (newyork.dmevals.local as DC), 14 event 4768 TGT requests all show PreAuthType 2 and TicketEncryptionType 0x12 (AES256), and all 28 event 4769 TGS requests are also 0x12 with Status 0x0. The krbtgt service tickets requested (by pbeesly and by SCRANTON$) are normal TGT-renewal patterns, not forged tickets. The only LSASS full-access reads were by PowerShell on scranton (see T1558 finding) — a prerequisite for krbtgt theft, but no forged-TGT authentication, no RC4/0x17 downgrade, and no Kerberos error events (only KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED in Zeek, which is normal pre-auth negotiation) were observed.

findings.title: No silver-ticket indicators: service tickets are AES256 for host accounts only, no forged service-ticket use
findings.summary: The 28 event 4769 TGS requests on newyork.dmevals.local target only machine accounts (NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, SCRANTON$, WEC$) and krbtgt, all with TicketEncryptionType 0x12 (AES256) and Status 0x0. There is no RC4 (0x17) downgrade, no unusual SPN targeting, and no service-account ticket anomalies that would indicate a forged silver ticket. Zeek kerberos records (separate 2020-04-30 window) likewise show only AES256 cifs/host/ldap/HTTP TGS requests by pbeesly, all successful.

findings.title: No Kerberoasting: no RC4 TGS requests and no bulk SPN enumeration by any account

In this window all 28 TGS requests are AES256 (0x12), requested by pbeesly and SCRANTON$ for a small set of machine accounts, and no PowerShell script blocks or process command lines referencing SPN enumeration, GetUserSPNs, Invoke-Kerberoast or Rubeus were found. The Zeek kerberos log (2020-04-30) shows only routine AES256 TGS requests for cifs/host/ldap/HTTP services.

findings.title: No AS-REP roasting: every TGT request used pre-authentication
findings.summary: AS-REP roasting requires TGT requests for accounts without Kerberos pre-authentication. All 14 event 4768 records on newyork.dmevals.local show PreAuthType 2 (pre-auth enabled) with Status 0x0, for pbeesly and SCRANTON$. The Zeek kerberos log shows the expected KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED followed by a successful AES256 AS exchange for pbeesly — normal pre-auth negotiation, not roasting. No asreproast/GetNPUsers/Rubeus command lines or script blocks were found.

findings.title: No SAML token forging observed; logon packages are Kerberos/Negotiate only
findings.summary: Across 297 successful 4624 logons in windows.security the authentication packages are Kerberos (217), Negotiate (78), NTLM (1) and one unset value, with logon processes Kerberos, Advapi, User32, NtLmSsp and one unset - no SAML, ADFS or token-based authentication package appears. A search of windows.security for SAML/ADFS/token object and service names returned only Credential Manager 5379 events for WindowsLive token/cert and MicrosoftAccount targets, which are stored-credential reads, not forged SAML assertions. No SAML token forging was observed.

findings.title: WebDAV 401 challenge/response burst from 10.0.1.4 to 192.168.0.4 is Windows WebDAV-MiniRedir, not MFA request generation
findings.summary: The only T1621-relevant hits were 62 zeek HTTP events, all between 10.0.1.4 and 192.168.0.4:80 (single destination, single source). The 31 HTTP 401 responses flagged by the stacking check are the normal WebDAV authentication handshake: every request is issued by user agent 'Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362' and each 401 is immediately followed by a successful retry on the same URI (e.g. OPTIONS /webdav 401 -> 301, PROPFIND /webdav/ 401 -> 207, PUT /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z 401 -> 201, LOCK 401 -> 200, HEAD 401 -> 200, PROPPATCH 401 -> 207, UNLOCK 401 -> 204). The session ends with a successful PUT of /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z (201 Created) and a LOCK/UNLOCK cycle, i.e. a file copy to a WebDAV share, not repeated authentication challenges to an identity provider. No MFA/identity-provider infrastructure is present anywhere in the data: all 53 DNS queries resolve only internal AD names (newyork/nashua/scranton.dmevals.local, wec.dmevals.local, _ldap._tcp...) and Microsoft/Windows Update/azureedge endpoints, and all 378 TLS records have client server_name 192.168.0.4 (no okta/duo/azure-mfa style endpoint). On the Windows side there is no MFA activity either: zero 4625 failed logons, zero PowerShell script blocks referencing MFA/2FA/Authenticator, and the only two script-block matches for 'azure' are the benign Microsoft xActiveDirectory DSC module manifest (C:\Program Files\WindowsPowerShell\Modules\xActiveDirectory\xActiveDirectory.psd1) loaded by SYSTEM on newyork.dmevals.local. 4624 logons are ordinary (218 network Kerberos, 61 service, 15 interactive, 2 remote-interactive). No evidence of MFA fatigue/push bombing or MFA request generation.
